blocks.text: Every BST operation starts the same way: stand at the root, compare, and go **left** if the value is smaller or **right** if it's bigger. Searching stops when it finds the value; inserting keeps going until it falls off the tree, and puts the new node in that empty spot. Both can be written **recursively** or with a **loop** — this lesson shows both, plus the two easiest searches of all, the minimum and the maximum.

blocks.alt: Searching for 7 in the tree with root 8: 7 is less than 8 so go left to 3, 7 is more than 3 so go right to 6, 7 is more than 6 so go right and find 7. Four nodes are checked; the right subtree of 8 and the left subtree of 3 are never looked at. Inserting 5 follows 8, 3, 6, 4 and becomes the right child of 4.

elements.text: one comparison per level: left if smaller, right if bigger
elements.originalText: one comparison per level: left if smaller, right if bigger

blocks.text: Compare the target with the node. Equal: found. Smaller: it can only be in the **left** subtree. Bigger: only in the **right**. If you reach an empty child, the value isn't in the tree. The recursive version reads like the definition; the loop does the same walk with no call stack, so it uses O(1) memory.

blocks.caption: Each comparison throws away a whole side of the tree.

blocks.text: **Time O(h)** either way. **Space O(h)** for the recursion's call stack, **O(1)** for the loop.

The smallest value is as far **left** as you can go: every step left reaches something smaller, and a node with no left child has nothing smaller below it. The largest is as far **right** as you can go. No comparisons needed at all.
**Time O(h), space O(1).** In the tree above: the minimum is 1 (8 → 3 → 1) and the maximum is 14 (8 → 10 → 14).

Inserting is a search for a value that isn't there: follow the comparisons until the next step would leave the tree, and hang the new node on that empty side. The new node is always a **leaf**, and nothing else in the tree moves. The recursive version returns each subtree's (possibly new) root and re-attaches it on the way back up; the loop remembers the **parent** so it can attach the new node to it.

blocks.caption: The new value follows the comparisons down and becomes a leaf where the path runs out.

blocks.text: **Time O(h)**; **space O(h)** recursive, **O(1)** with the loop.

blocks.alt: Recursive search / insert: O(h) time, O(h) space. Loop search / insert: O(h) time, O(1) space. Min / max: O(h) time, O(1) space.

items: **Recursion** is shorter and mirrors the definition — the usual choice in interviews.
**Loops** use no call stack, which matters when the tree can be very tall (a skewed tree with 100,000 nodes would overflow most call stacks).
Both cost **O(h)**: about log₂ n steps in a balanced tree, up to n in a skewed one.
